data.title: How Women Can Protect Their Nest Egg From a Late-Career Layoff — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Zaneilia Harris

One of my clients, a senior executive with a major health insurance company, dreamed of retirement and planned for it for years. When she came to me in her mid-50s, she had done all the right things: locked in her savings rate, fully funded her retirement accounts, and decided on an approximate retirement age of 62-or 65 if she still enjoyed the work.

But before she could reach that goal, the company restructured its leadership and her position was eliminated.

Unfortunately, my client's experience isn't unique in the current economic environment. For many women, especially Black women, the path to retirement isn't linear. More than 455,000 women left the workforce during the first eight months of 2025, according to data from Catalyst, with those from marginalized racial and ethnic groups disproportionately affected by layoffs compared with their white counterparts.

For many women, their 50s are peak earning years, which makes it especially discouraging when unexpected employment changes occur. When a woman's income disappears unexpectedly, I encourage her to take some time to absorb what's happened. That's what I did with my client laid off from her health insurance role. We came together to reassess the financial plan and take stock of current assets, investment accounts, monthly spending and cash flow, healthcare costs, tax implications, income sources, and legacy goals.

Social Security questions. Although my client and I hadn't discussed a scenario that included forced retirement by age 60, at a meeting a year prior to the layoff I told her to build up her emergency cash reserves to cover two years, well beyond the three- to six-month rule of thumb. That extra cushion helped keep her nest egg intact, as did that fact that over the years she'd never touched her retirement savings.

Women often plan to delay Social Security to maximize their monthly benefit in retirement. When income disappears without warning, many end up claiming early simply because they need the money. Before any withdrawal decision gets made, I walk clients through a "buckets of money" framework to think through which accounts to draw from first, how each withdrawal is taxed, which assets to preserve, how to avoid any unnecessary taxes, and how to build income that lasts.

In this client's case, that foundation had already been laid. During her working years, I encouraged her to pursue contributions to her Roth 401(k), building in flexibility before her plans changed. When the layoff came and her income temporarily dropped, that dip created an opening: room to convert traditional IRA assets to Roth at a lower tax rate than she would have paid if she was still earning her full salary. That reduced her future required minimum distributions from her IRA and created more tax-free income later in retirement.

Shock absorbers. I don't build a retirement plan around a date on the calendar, I build it to absorb whatever comes up before that date arrives. Being well prepared, and helping clients take ownership of that preparation, can make a major difference in how a disrupted retirement plan holds up, as it did for my client.

I often check in with my clients informally, not just at the scheduled review, to get a sense of their current vision for retirement, and to reassess evolving priorities around money, knowing that money is a tool clients use to get where they want to go.

That groundwork lets a client trust her own judgment when an unexpected circumstance arrives. It allows her to picture what she wants, and feel steady no matter what decision she's facing.

Zaneilia Harris, CFP, is president of Harris & Harris Wealth Management Group. She helps women achieve their dreams and solve their financial challenges. She is the author of "Finance 'n Stilettos: Money Matters for the Well-Heeled Woman." In her 20-plus year career in finance and accounting she has worked with Merrill Lynch, Edward Jones Investments, PricewaterhouseCoopers, and the Nasdaq Stock Market.

data.title: AI stock concentration nears past bubble peaks
data.description:
Key points:
  • Main US indexes rally, but off highs; Nasdaq out front, up ~1.3%
  • Consumer discretionary leads S&P 500 sector gainers; healthcare weakest group
  • Dollar, gold down ~1%; US crude falls >1%; bitcoin gains
  • US 10-year Treasury yield rises to ~5.27%

AI STOCK CONCENTRATION NEARS PAST BUBBLE PEAKS

Investors who think the artificial intelligence rally has further to run can find support in the 19th-century railroad boom, Bank of America analysts led by Michael Hartnett said in a note. But they warned that the comparison also points to risks.

The 10 biggest AI stocks now make up 42% of the market. That's within the 36% to 44% range at which major bubbles have topped out, from the 1920s to the dotcom boom in 2000. The exception was railroads, which hit 63% in 1881.

That means the bull case depends on the idea that "it's the railroads this time," the analysts wrote.

Some signs support that view, they said. AI capital spending is 3.5% to 4% of GDP, still below the roughly 5% peak of the railroad era. And while freight rates were falling before railroad stocks peaked, semiconductor prices are now soaring.

Other signs don't. The railroad boom happened while US Treasury yields were falling, and it ended because of credit and liquidity crises. Today, yields are rising instead, with zero-coupon bonds down 15% in the third quarter.

data.title: Ireland lowers forecast for 2026 budget surplus to €6.9 billion
data.description:
Key points:
  • Cuts to excise duties on fuels in place until next year
  • Lower 2026 corporate tax forecast more than made up in 2027
  • Jump in September corporate tax receipts a timing issue

Ireland expects to run a budget surplus of €6.9 billion ($7.8 billion) this year, lower than the €9.2 billion forecast in April before the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overruns, finance ministry data showed on Friday.

Ireland introduced cuts to excise duties on fuels in March and plans to keep them partly or fully in place until at least the end of February next year. Ministers will provide an update on the timing in Tuesday's budget for next year.

The finance ministry also lowered its forecast for corporate tax revenue for 2026 to €34.1 billion from the €35.3 billion estimated in April, but hiked its estimate for 2027 to €39 billion from €37.4 billion previously.

A surge in corporate tax has helped drive overall tax revenues to record levels for each of the last five years. These will fund another large annual budget package of tax cuts and spending increases next week, a rarity in Europe where many countries' public finances are stretched.

Corporate tax receipts, which are mainly paid by a small number of US multinationals, jumped to €4.9 billion in September compared with €1.8 billion in the same month a year ago. However, the surge partly reflects a timing factor, the finance ministry said, adding that there would be corresponding decreases in some of the remaining months.

The tax return data also showed that Ireland's strongly growing economy continues to push up the other two main tax categories, with income tax and VAT receipts up 7.8% and 8.9% respectively so far this year. Irish modified domestic demand (MDD), officials' preferred measure of economic activity, grew by 3.1% year-on-year in the first half of 2026 and by 4.7% last year.

Total tax receipts year-to-date were up 10.7% when one-off proceeds of Apple back taxes are excluded.

Government spending this year was up 7.7% year-on-year to €83.4 billion by the end of September, the data showed, with expenditure on day-to-day services growing at a faster pace than investment in public infrastructure.

data.title: Canadian dollar extends weekly losing streak as interest rate spreads widen
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

The Canadian dollar added to its weekly decline against the US dollar on Friday as oil prices fell and interest rate spreads between the US and Canada continued to widen.

The loonie was trading 0.3% lower at 1.4257 per US dollar, or 70.14 US cents, after moving in a range of 1.4202 to 1.42595. On Thursday, the currency touched an 18-month low at 1.4263.

  • For the week, the loonie was down 0.8%, which would be its fourth straight weekly decline, as the greenback extended recent gains against a basket of major currencies.

  • "Rising oil prices and concerns that inflation could remain stubborn have put pressure on global central banks to take a more hawkish stance," said Sarah Ying, head of foreign exchange strategy at CIBC Capital Markets.

  • "The US is still believed to be relatively better off relative to the rest of the world, and fiscal concerns in Europe are leaving little alternative other than to flock to the greenback," she said.

  • US job growth slowed more than expected in September and the nonfarm payrolls count for the prior two months was revised sharply lower, almost taking another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve this month off the table.

  • Still, the Canadian 2-year yield fell 4 basis points further below the equivalent US rate to a gap of about 157 basis points, its widest since February 2025.

  • The US price of oil, one of Canada's major exports, gave back some of the previous day's advance as Group of Seven countries agreed on the release of 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves. US crude oil futures were trading 1.6% lower at $91.40 a barrel.

  • The Canadian 10-year yield (CA10YT=RR) was up nearly 1 basis point to 3.940% but remained below a nearly three-year high touched during Thursday's session at 4.042%.

data.title: Judge warns AI could stunt lawyers' training and harm their clients
data.description:
By Mike Scarcella

A federal judge has warned that law firms' increasing use of artificial intelligence could create risks for clients and hinder the training of junior lawyers, even as he declined to sanction attorneys over AI-generated errors in a court filing.

Manhattan-based US District Judge Arun Subramanian said in an order this week that the episode should serve as a "wakeup call" for lawyers, cautioning that AI-generated legal work must be carefully checked for accuracy.

"While clients may demand the use of AI to save money, there is a risk of adverse consequences when things go wrong," Subramanian wrote. "For this reason, it might make sense to clients to think hard before requiring counsel to use AI for tasks such as the drafting of briefs." The judge did not say the client in this case had requested its lawyers use AI.

State and federal judges increasingly are weighing whether and how to sanction lawyers over their misuse of AI as the technology becomes more widespread.

In the New York case, Subramanian in an order last month questioned whether "unchecked" use of AI led to citation errors in a copyright infringement case he was overseeing.

The judge this week declined to impose sanctions on the lawyers after Cynthia Arato, an attorney for defendant Foundation Media, apologized and said the errors stemmed from another lawyer at her firm who was responsible for preparing the initial draft and finalizing it before it was filed.

Arato said in a declaration this week that the lawyer, who was not named in Arato's declaration, acted "contrary to the firm's policies and training" and that the failure to check AI-generated citations was "an isolated error and not any bad faith or intent to mislead or deceive the court."

Foundation Media declined to comment. There was no indication in court filings that the company had directed its outside lawyers to use AI.

Arato said her firm, Shapiro Arato Bach, was implementing further safeguards against AI misuse.

In a filing submitted on Thursday, Arato disclosed that the firm had used AI tools created by technology company Harvey to help prepare the improperly vetted filing.

Harvey did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Subramanian said in his order that the legal profession should "think about ways to ensure that junior lawyers are getting the training they need, even as reliance on these technological tools increases." He suggested that firms could require initial drafts of briefs to be prepared without AI assistance.

"The use of AI may be unavoidable, but mentoring young lawyers is a joint responsibility that we all share," Subramanian wrote.

data.title: Amazon Stock Rises on $1 Billion AWS Data Center Push
data.description:
Shares of Amazon climbed about 1.5% in Friday morning trading after its cloud unit said it plans to invest more than $1 billion over five years in U.S. communities that host its data centers.

Amazon Web Services said the initiative will support local priorities including education, workforce development, energy affordability, and conservation efforts involving water and electricity, according to a Friday press release.

The spending comes as the expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence workloads has drawn scrutiny over power demand, utility costs and water consumption. AWS said more than 100 proposals for data-center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S.

Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers from 2011 through 2025, with major projects or expansions underway in several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi.

AWS also said it aims to become water positive across its data-center network by 2030, meaning it intends to return more water to local communities than it consumes. The company said it has completed 75% of the work toward that goal.

data.title: European shares rebound after bond rout on easing Fed rate-hike bets
data.description:
Key points:
  • Julius Baer gains after share buyback programme
  • IG Group drops over 22% after cutting annual revenue forecast
  • Technology shares lead sectoral gains, up 2.6%

By Sudeshna Ghoshal and Purvi Agarwal

European stocks rebounded on Friday, after a bond-driven selloff, as retreating oil prices and softer-than-expected US jobs data eased expectations for near-term rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

The pan-European STOXX 600 closed 0.8% higher, after touching its lowest in more than three months on Thursday.

US job growth slowed more than expected in September and figures for the prior two months were revised sharply downward, prompting traders to pull back on US rate hike bets for October.

"Markets dodged a bullet with a weaker-than-expected jobs report likely taking an October Fed rate hike off the table," said Ronald Temple, managing director of Lazard Asset Management.

"But with two more months of inflation data to be released before the December meeting, the Fed will be compelled to tighten policy again."

Bond yields declined, with the one on the German 10-year bond (DE10YT=RR), a benchmark for the euro zone, down over 6 basis points at 3.454%. Oil prices also fell by $3 a barrel, further aiding risk appetite.

The surge in global government bond yields has battered equities in recent weeks, leaving investors averse to risk assets. Despite gains in the session, the STOXX 600 posted weekly declines.

Most sectors ended in positive territory on Friday, with renewed AI enthusiasm putting technology stocks (.SX8P) in the lead.

AT & S Austria Technologies & Systemtechnik gained 10%, Infineon Technologies was up about 9%, while Aixtron and Soitec added 7.6% each.

European banking stocks (.SX7P) were little changed on Friday but registered their biggest weekly fall since April, hurt by concerns about higher interest rates denting the economy.

Meanwhile, data showed euro zone inflation surged more than expected in September and is likely to rise further in the coming months.

The ECB lifted interest rates last month, and traders are currently pricing in 81.8% chances of a rate hike in December, LSEG data showed.

"Higher interest rates combined with elevated inflation are a negative for equities, but whether equity markets will react badly depends on how long investors feel the problem will last," said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar.

France presented its 2027 budget on Thursday, seeking to enact unpopular belt-tightening measures aimed at reducing the deficit and reassuring the bond market ahead of next year's presidential elections.

Late last month, France's 10-year borrowing costs (FR10YT=RR) reached the highest since the global financial crisis in 2008.

Among stocks, London's IG Group slid 22.6% to the bottom of the STOXX 600 after the online trading firm cut its annual revenue forecast due to subdued trading volatility.

It was IG's biggest one-day drop since December 2016.

Julius Baer rose 2% after the Swiss bank announced a share buyback programme of up to 600 million Swiss francs ($724 million).

data.title: Gigasun announces preliminary outcome of the Company’s Rights Issue
data.description:
Gigasun AB (publ) (“Gigasun” or the “Company”) announces the preliminary outcome of the Company’s rights issue (the “Rights Issue”), for which the subscription period ended on 1 October 2026. The preliminary outcome indicates that approximately 68.4 percent of the Rights Issue has been subscribed for, corresponding to total subscription proceeds of approximately SEK 69.9 million. Of the subscription proceeds, approximately SEK 60.6 million will be paid by way of set-off against existing claims on the Company and approximately SEK 9.3 million will be paid in cash before deduction of costs attributable to the Rights Issue.

The preliminary outcome indicates that 55,061,708 shares, corresponding to approximately 67.4 percent of the Rights Issue, have been subscribed for with the support of subscription rights. In addition, applications to subscribe for 836,673 shares without the support of subscription rights have been received, corresponding to approximately 1.0 percent of the Rights Issue. Accordingly, the preliminary outcome indicates that a total of 55,898,381 shares, corresponding to approximately 68.4 percent of the Rights Issue, have been subscribed for with and without the support of subscription rights.

The subscription price in the Rights Issue is SEK 1.25 per share, corresponding to total subscription proceeds of approximately SEK 69.9 million based on the preliminary outcome. Of this amount, approximately SEK 60.6 million will be paid by way of set-off against existing claims on the Company and approximately SEK 9.3 million in cash. The costs attributable to the Rights Issue are estimated to amount to approximately SEK 1.5–2.0 million.

Based on the preliminary outcome, Gigasun’s share capital will increase by SEK 11,179,676.20, from SEK 11,439,445.00 to SEK 22,619,121.20, through the issuance of 55,898,381 new shares. Following the Rights Issue, the total number of shares in Gigasun will amount to 113,095,606.

Those who have subscribed for shares without the support of subscription rights will be allocated shares in accordance with the principles set out in the information document published by the Company on 8 September 2026. Notification of allocation to persons who have subscribed for shares without the support of subscription rights is expected to be distributed by means of a settlement note within approximately one week. Allocated shares shall be paid for in cash in accordance with the instructions set out in the settlement note. Investors who have subscribed through a nominee will receive notification of allocation in accordance with the procedures of their respective nominee. Only those who have been allocated shares will be notified.

The final outcome of the Rights Issue is expected to be announced within approximately one week.

Issuing agent

Aqurat Fondkommission AB is acting as issuing agent in connection with the Rights Issue.

Important information

This press release does not constitute an offer or invitation to acquire or subscribe for securities in Gigasun in any jurisdiction.

This press release does not constitute a prospectus within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 of the European Parliament and of the Council (the “Prospectus Regulation”). The Rights Issue is not subject to the requirement to publish a prospectus pursuant to the Prospectus Regulation. In connection with the Rights Issue, the Company has prepared information documents which are available on the Company’s website.

About the operation

Gigasun operates in China through its wholly owned subsidiaries Advanced Soltech Renewable Energy (Hangzhou) Co. Ltd (“ASRE”) and Longrui Solar Energy (Suqian) Co. Ltd. (“SQ”), and Suqian Ruiyan New Energy Co., Ltd. (“RY”).

The customer does not pay for the solar PV installation, but instead enters an agreement to buy the electricity that the solar PV installation produces under a 20-year agreement. Current income comes from the sale of electricity to customers and governmental subsidies.

The goal is to have an installed capacity of 1,000 megawatts (MW) in the medium term.
